# Working in this repository

Axylo is a browser charting library. The product is specified in `docs/02-product-spec.md`; the build plan is `docs/03-plan-typescript-release.md`. Read the sections your task names before writing code.

## Rules for every change

- **Contracts are fixed.** `packages/axylo/src/core/contracts.ts` and `packages/axylo/src/public.ts` are the interfaces between modules. Do not edit them. If your work needs a change there, stop that part, finish what you can, and describe the exact change you need in your report.
- **Stay in your files.** Each task lists the directories it owns. Do not create, edit or delete anything else, including configuration and other modules. Several agents work in this checkout at the same time.
- **No runtime dependencies.** Use the platform (`Intl`, typed arrays). Dev dependencies already installed: TypeScript, Vitest, fast-check, esbuild, Playwright (system Chrome), axe-core. The network is not available; do not try to install anything.
- **No DOM at import time.** A module that needs the DOM takes it as a parameter or touches it inside a function. Pure stages (data, scales, formatting, layout, scene) must run in Node.
- **Hot paths use typed arrays.** No object per data point, no array of arrays per data point, no copying of large columns that the contracts say are borrowed.
- **Never guess silently.** Anything that cannot be drawn as given is reported through the `DiagnosticSink` with the code from spec section 3.5.
- **Tests come from the spec.** Expected values are derived from the specification and the fixture data, never by running the implementation and pasting its output. Use fast-check property tests for invariants ("for any data …"). A test you cannot make pass is reported as failing; do not weaken it or change its expected value.
- **TypeScript strict, no `any`** in exported signatures. `__DEV__` is a build-time boolean (true in tests).
- **Comments say why**, not what. Names are plain words.
- **Do not commit.** The coordinator commits.

## Commands

```bash
npm run typecheck      # tsc over the library, its tests, and the API examples in docs/api
npm test               # unit and property tests (Node)
npm run build          # packages/axylo/dist
npm run test:browser   # browser tests against the built bundle, in system Chrome
```

## Your report

End with a short report: what you built (files), what you verified and how (paste the last lines of the test run), what is not done or not verified, any contract change you need, and any place where the spec was ambiguous and what you assumed. Keep "ran and saw" apart from "expect".
# Decision 0002: SVG draws the marks in 1.0

Status: **final for 1.0**, confirmed by the owner on 2026-11-22. All shipped chart types draw marks with SVG. The benchmark harness retains the old Canvas records and can replay the renderer decision on the original sealed artifact.

## Release evidence

- The software family selected SVG under [rule 3](../04-plan-performance.md#51-declared-endpoints-provisional-until-the-pilot). Eight timing endpoints were too noisy to distinguish the renderers by the declared tolerances. Neither renderer had a late streaming run. The old Canvas implementation added 2,269 bytes gzipped in the matched script-tag measurement, above rule 3’s 512-byte cutoff. [Software decision](../../bench/decision/no-idle-2026-11-21/decision-renderer-20261121T143350Z.json)
- The GPU family returned no decision because the dashboard GPU-memory result depended on run order. Canvas took less main-thread time on both GPU resize workloads beyond the tolerance, with neither difference reaching the worthwhile margin. [GPU decision](../../bench/decision/no-idle-2026-11-21/decision-gpu-20261121T143402Z.json)
- Both families ran on Chrome 158.0.8127.36 on the same reference desktop, using artifact `20261119T091624Z-b643862f-b78698`. The owner accepted the 2026-11-21 measurements and dropped the idle-machine rule. Load is recorded with the results. [Benchmark method](../../bench/README.md)

The SVG implementation uses CSS paint expressions for live theme changes and retains the plot's device-pixel geometry. 1.0 has no Canvas marks option. HTML text, accessibility, hit testing and streaming remain independent of the mark renderer.

The packed consumer bundles shrank by 2,487 gzipped bytes for all chart types (118,252 to 115,765) and 1,646 for the line-only entry (98,627 to 96,981). These before-and-after pack measurements include the related removal of the switch and Canvas-only styles.

## Historical M1 review and measurements

The table below is kept as measured. These statements made from it in the first version are withdrawn or narrowed:

- **Withdrawn: "nothing measured favours canvas except all-thread CPU during resize."** The recorded heap, DOM-node and layout counts also favour canvas.
- **Withdrawn: the resize CPU gap is raster work.** The number is CPU for the whole renderer process; no stage was traced.
- **Withdrawn: simplification bounds every chart by its width.** It was shown for line series only; point marks and many-series charts were not measured.
- **Withdrawn: an SVG theme change needs no run-time work.** Both renderers recorded six DOM mutations per toggle; "no canvas drawing call" is all that was observed.
- **Withdrawn: normalization and garbage collection explain the gap to uPlot.** About 71–73% of busy time in the production profiles is unmapped; the normalization share comes from development builds. It is a hypothesis to test, not a finding.
- **Narrowed: "half the renderer memory."** The halving is of the increase above a data-only page at pixel ratio 2 (34.2 → 17.7 MiB). Absolute renderer memory was 74.7 → 56.2 MiB, and at pixel ratio 1 the increase was 23.1 → 18.4 MiB.
- **Narrowed: "no frame later than 25 ms."** True of the recorded animation-frame callbacks; the window can miss an interval that spans its boundary, and a callback is not a presented frame.
- **Void: every 24-chart page row** (page at pixel ratio 1 and 2, resize of the 24-chart page, and the memory row). The harness fix pass found that these runs drew no marks: at 230 × 115 px each tile is below the 120 × 80 px plot minimum of spec L8, so every chart showed its text fallback. The SVG records carry `svgPaths: 0`; the canvas runs held empty canvases. The numbers compare two empty charts and say nothing about the renderers. The harness now rejects a run whose chart drew no marks, and the page workload uses 340 × 200 px tiles.
- **Narrowed: verdicts.** 149 metric comparisons were judged without adjustment for choosing among them, on six pairs or fewer per workload, with noise bands from one session and two workload shapes. Two "SVG lower" rows allow a gain as small as 0.16 ms (10,000 points) and 6.3 ms (dashboard at pixel ratio 2).

Evidence: [bench/results/m1-renderer-comparison.md](../../bench/results/m1-renderer-comparison.md). One session of 39 runs, production build, headless Chrome 157, machine under load from other work, A-versus-A noise bands for two workloads only.

### What M1 measured

Canvas → SVG, medians of main-thread task time unless stated. "Lower" means the 95% interval cleared zero and the noise band where one existed.

| Workload | Canvas | SVG | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Streaming, per update | 2.26 ms | 1.45 ms | SVG lower |
| Theme change, per toggle | 2.68 ms and 27 drawing calls | 2.01 ms and no drawing call | SVG lower |
| Resize, one chart of 100,000 points | 915 ms | 472 ms | SVG lower on the main thread |
| Same, CPU across all threads | 1,035 ms | 1,770 ms | **SVG higher** |
| Resize, 24-chart page | 730 ms | 525 ms | Void: no marks were drawn |
| First chart, 10,000 points | 34.0 ms | 28.4 ms | SVG lower |
| 24-chart page at pixel ratio 2 | 199 ms | 158 ms | Void: no marks were drawn |
| First chart, 3 × 120 | 23.6 ms | 19.8 ms | Inconclusive |
| First chart, 100,000 points | 81.8 ms | 83.5 ms | Inconclusive |
| First chart, 1,000,000 points | 622 ms | 652 ms | Inconclusive (4 blocks) |
| Memory, 24-chart page at pixel ratio 2 | 34.2 MiB renderer, 11.5 MiB GPU, 7.7 MiB backing stores | 17.7 MiB, 2.2 MiB, none | Void: no marks were drawn |

No frame was later than 25 ms in any configuration, so frame pacing does not separate the two.

### Why SVG was the working default

1. On the line workloads measured, main-thread task time was lower with SVG or the two could not be told apart.
2. Line series are simplified to a few vertices per pixel column before either renderer sees them, so for line charts the path size follows the plot width, not the data.
3. SVG follows the page with less code: forced colors and print work through CSS, browser zoom stays sharp, and there is no backing store to size, cap or lose. This is a design argument, not a measurement.

### What M1 did not establish

- **GPU rasterization was not measured.** Headless Chrome here does not use a GPU. The resize, pixel-ratio-2 and process-memory results need a headed, GPU-backed rerun before they transfer.
- **Dense point marks were not measured.** A scatter chart with tens of thousands of markers is the case most likely to favour canvas.
- **One browser, one machine, one session.** Firefox and Safari may order the two differently.
- **Many series, pan and zoom, and the budget workloads P4, P7 and P8 were not measured**, and the million-point comparison has four pairs.
- Both renderers are far from uPlot in the configurations measured (about 80 ms against 12 ms at 100,000 points; uPlot draws no tooltip or accessibility layer). Where that time goes is not established.
# Decision 0004: where the tooltip goes, and when the focused point's text changes

Status: decided by the coordinator on 2026-11-18 after the second review of the interaction layer (`reviews/2026-11-18/impl/wp/core3.interaction.review.md`, new findings 3 and 4). Not rehearsed with a screen reader or a screen magnifier; both parts need that before they are called verified.

## 1. The tooltip is anchored to the datum and never takes the pointer (revision 3)

Revision 1 (placed across the reading axis, offset from the pointer, interactive while hovered) was implemented three times and still failed the acceptance tests: because the tooltip's position followed the pointer it moved away when approached, because it took pointer events it stalled the readout or swallowed the click whenever a move landed on it, and it could cover controls and the focus ring. Revision 2 removes the causes instead of tuning distances. Revision 3 (after the final review, `reviews/2026-11-18/impl/wp/core-final.interaction.review.md`) replaces revision 2's separate hold rules with one, and adds rules 8 to 10 and the limits in rules 5 and 6.

**Problem.** WCAG 1.4.13 requires content shown on hover to stay when the pointer moves onto it. Spec I1 requires the readout to name the datum at the pointer on every move, the tooltip not to cover the active mark, to stay inside the viewport, and to fall back to a fixed readout when it cannot fit. On a line chart the whole plot picks, so anything that takes pointer events inside the plot blocks picking.

**Rules.**

1. **Position depends on the datum only.** For the datum on show, the tooltip is placed against the bounding box of that datum's active marks (all series at that x for line, area and bar; the point for scatter; the slice for donut), enlarged by the focus ring's width. The pointer's own position never enters the computation, so the tooltip does not move while the datum is unchanged, and it cannot run away from an approaching pointer.
2. **Candidates, in order:** above the box, below it, then to the right and to the left of it (for horizontal bars: right, left, above, below). Along the other axis it is centred on the box and shifted only as far as needed. A candidate is valid when the tooltip lies wholly inside the plot rectangle, inside the viewport and inside every clipping ancestor, and overlaps neither the box nor any control. The first valid candidate is used. For a donut the first candidate is the hole, when the tooltip fits inside it.
3. **A hovered tooltip never takes pointer events.** It is `pointer-events: none`. The plot keeps receiving every move, so picking never stalls at any speed, and a click goes to the plot and selects the datum under the pointer. Moving the pointer onto the tooltip therefore cannot hide it: on line, area and bar the tooltip stays for as long as the pointer's position along the reading axis still picks the same datum, which a straight approach across the reading axis does; on scatter and donut, while the pointer is inside the tooltip's rectangle the datum is held (computed from coordinates in the plot's own move handler, not by letting the tooltip take the event).
3b. **A rest holds the datum along the way to the content (revision 3).** Rule 3 alone lets the content change whenever the straight path to it crosses positions that pick something else, and the final review found such paths for every placement: a tooltip beside a tall bar, a donut's tooltip in the hole, a scatter point's tooltip, a tooltip above a point in a dense line near the plot's edge, and the strip under a small plot. So one rule covers all of them, replacing the per-placement cases of revision 2 (including the unconditional hold inside a scatter or donut tooltip's rectangle, which is withdrawn): once the pointer has rested on a datum for 250 ms (no move larger than 2 CSS px, measured in viewport pixels), that datum is held while the pointer stays inside the corridor between its resting position and the rectangle of the content shown for it (the floating tooltip, or the strip in readout mode), that is, the convex hull of the point and the rectangle, and inside the rectangle itself. Leaving the corridor resumes picking on that same move. A pointer that has not rested is never held, in any placement, so a sweep never stalls.
   - **The hold affects what is shown, never what is activated.** A click or tap always picks afresh from the pointer's position; if that is a different datum from the one held, the click selects and pins the datum under the pointer. A click on empty space (a donut's hole, outside a scatter point's radius) selects nothing.
   - **The hold belongs to one datum, one geometry and one presentation.** It ends when the displayed frame changes that datum's anchor or the content's rectangle, when the presentation switches between floating and strip, on a pin, on Escape, when the pointer leaves the plot and the content, and on any rebuild. After it ends, picking is from the pointer's position at once, without waiting for a move.
4. **Rows are not controls while hovered.** A hovered tooltip is text. Clicking or tapping the plot pins the tooltip for that datum; a pinned tooltip takes pointer events, stays until Escape, a click elsewhere, or its datum leaves the displayed frame, and its rows are buttons of at least 24 × 24 CSS px (WCAG 2.5.8) that select a series. Keyboard focus shows the same tooltip by the same placement; it is never over the focus ring because the box includes the ring.
   - *Revision 3 addendum (two-click range, spec I4):* while the toolbar's Select range toggle is pressed, a click or tap on the plot sets one end of the zoom range instead and neither pins nor selects, and Escape releases the toggle (in rule 7's order after a drag, before a tooltip or a pin).
5. **Readout mode is decided by layout, not by hover.** When the plot, laid out without a strip, would be narrower than 240 CSS px or shorter than 140 CSS px, the figure is in readout mode: a strip of two text lines (two actual line heights of the strip's own font, whatever the page's text size) is reserved under the plot in the layout, and the content that would be in the tooltip is written there as running text ("x: series value; series value; +N more"), wrapping to the two lines and ending in "+N more" when it does not fit; at least the x and one row are always shown. The strip is part of the figure's flow: it covers nothing and nothing covers it. In readout mode there is no floating tooltip. A pinned datum makes the strip's entries buttons of 24 px height. If reserving the strip would leave the plot under the minimum of spec L8 (80 px high), no strip is reserved and pointing shows no readout at all: the datum is still highlighted, and its values are in the keyboard reading and the table. Such a plot is never put into floating mode.
6. **When no candidate is valid outside readout mode** (a tooltip taller than the room around a tall stack, for example), rows are dropped from the end and counted in "+N more" until a candidate is valid. The tooltip is never wider or taller than the visible part of the plot (its content wraps; the visible part is the plot rectangle cut by the viewport and by every clipping ancestor's real clipping edge). If no candidate is valid with one row, the candidate that overlaps the active box least is used, shifted along its free axis as far as needed to avoid every control and every focus ring: controls and focus rings are never covered, in any case. This is the only case in which the active mark may be partly covered, and the table still has every value.
7. Escape dismisses a hovered or pinned tooltip without moving the pointer, until the pointer reaches a different datum. One Escape does one thing: while a tooltip, a pin or a drag is active, the chart consumes the key and nothing else reacts to it (a surrounding dialog stays open, single-series reading stays on); the next Escape goes to whatever is next.
8. **A pin is one datum.** The pin remembers the datum the reader chose. Other data that come to share its position are listed with it while it is displayed; when it leaves the displayed frame or is hidden, the pin ends, whatever else is at that position. A dismissal is remembered for that datum in the same way. With `tooltip: false` nothing can be pinned: a click still selects and takes focus.
9. **Pinned content is real.** A pinned tooltip or strip is exposed to assistive technology with its row buttons named by their text; rows keep their element across redraws while their identity is unchanged, so a press that spans a data update still completes.
10. **Coordinates.** Picking, anchors, clipping and placement use one mapping between the plot's layout pixels and viewport pixels, taken from fractional sizes, so a translated or scaled ancestor (any positive scale, uniform or not) is exact. Rotated, skewed or mirrored ancestors are not supported in 1.0; the limits section of the spec says so.

**Clarifications after the verification** (2026-11-18; the cross-provider check of revision 3, `reviews/2026-11-18/impl/wp/fixes-verify.interaction.review.md`, found these cases unstated; they add no rule, they say what the rules above mean there):

- *An x where no series has a mark* (every value at it is missing): rule 1 has no box to anchor to. The anchor is then the point at that x on the plot's vertical middle (for horizontal bars: at that category on the plot's horizontal middle).
- *The controls of rule 5 and the validity test of rule 2* are the chart's own controls, each taken with its painted focus outline. Controls of the page that happen to overlap the chart are outside what Axylo can know.
- *Several charts on one page and Escape (rule 7):* a chart spends an Escape only when focus is inside its figure, or, when focus is inside no chart, when it is the chart that most recently showed content. One key press is spent by at most one chart.
- *A key that leaves the reader on the same datum* (an arrow at the end of the data, Home on the first point) is not a move: it does not release a pin (rule 4) and does not rewrite the focused text (part 2).
- *A gesture and a pin:* starting a drag or a pinch ends the pin. No state exists in which a pin is held and nothing is shown.
- *A drag while Select range is pressed* zooms as a drag and releases the toggle: the range has been chosen.
- *After Escape from a hold* nothing opens at once: the held datum and the datum under the still pointer are both dismissed. A dismissed datum stays closed until the pointer reaches a datum other than itself (so after moving from one of the two onto the other, that other opens). Escape from a pin or from a plain hover dismisses only the datum on show, not whatever else the pointer is over. The pick itself is always current, so a click activates what is under the pointer.
- *The plot's focus ring* shows when the plot has focus and the last input to it was a key it handles, or when the browser matches `:focus-visible` (which the three engines do after a click on the plot as well). A ring after a click is accepted; what is required is that keyboard use always shows it.
- *Pointer positions are known to one CSS pixel.* Firefox and WebKit report mouse positions in whole pixels (a pointer at 336.96, 82.27 arrives as 336, 82), while the plot's edges and the corridor's edges are fractional. A position up to 1 CSS px outside the plot rectangle is therefore picked as if on its edge, and the corridor of rule 3b is taken with 1 px of slack, so a mark drawn on the plot's edge can be pointed at and a move along the corridor's edge stays inside it in every engine.

Rejected: revision 1; an interactive hovered tooltip with a "safe triangle" (still ambiguous when the reading axis and the approach coincide); always using the readout (loses the association between the values and the mark on plots that have room).

What "can itself be hovered" (spec I1) means under this decision, for the tests: the pointer can be moved straight from the datum onto the tooltip's rectangle, and the tooltip is still shown, for the same datum, when the pointer is inside it. It does not mean the tooltip is the hit-test target.

## 2. The focused point's text changes only for a reason the reader would name

**Problem.** The plot's keyboard proxy is a native range whose value text describes the focused point, ending with its position ("Point 4 of 120"). While data streams in, the count changes on every append, so the text of a focused control changes without the reader acting. Spec A7 forbids unrequested announcements; whether a given screen reader speaks such a change cannot be tested here.

**Rule.** The range's bounds and numeric value are always kept true to the displayed frame, silently. Its value text is rewritten only when:

1. the reader moves (a key, an assistive adjustment, a pointer or touch selection that takes focus),
2. the focused datum's own values change (the same x and series now read differently),
3. the focused datum leaves the frame (the text must then say where focus went), or
4. the plot regains focus.

An append that only changes the count or the ordinal of an unchanged datum does not rewrite the text. The position in the text can therefore be out of date until the next of the four events; it is recomputed then.

To check with a screen reader when one is available (added to decision 0001's list): idle appends with the plot focused are silent; an eviction of the focused point is spoken once; an increment immediately after an append lands on the expected neighbour and reads the current count.

# Decision 0004: where the tooltip goes, and when the focused point's text changes

Status: decided by the coordinator on 2026-11-18 after the second review of the interaction layer (`reviews/2026-11-18/impl/wp/core3.interaction.review.md`, new findings 3 and 4). Not rehearsed with a screen reader or a screen magnifier; both parts need that before they are called verified.

## 1. The tooltip is anchored to the datum and never takes the pointer (revision 3)

Revision 1 (placed across the reading axis, offset from the pointer, interactive while hovered) was implemented three times and still failed the acceptance tests: because the tooltip's position followed the pointer it moved away when approached, because it took pointer events it stalled the readout or swallowed the click whenever a move landed on it, and it could cover controls and the focus ring. Revision 2 removes the causes instead of tuning distances. Revision 3 (after the final review, `reviews/2026-11-18/impl/wp/core-final.interaction.review.md`) replaces revision 2's separate hold rules with one, and adds rules 8 to 10 and the limits in rules 5 and 6.

**Problem.** WCAG 1.4.13 requires content shown on hover to stay when the pointer moves onto it. Spec I1 requires the readout to name the datum at the pointer on every move, the tooltip not to cover the active mark, to stay inside the viewport, and to fall back to a fixed readout when it cannot fit. On a line chart the whole plot picks, so anything that takes pointer events inside the plot blocks picking.

**Rules.**

1. **Position depends on the datum only.** For the datum on show, the tooltip is placed against the bounding box of that datum's active marks (all series at that x for line, area and bar; the point for scatter; the slice for donut), enlarged by the focus ring's width. The pointer's own position never enters the computation, so the tooltip does not move while the datum is unchanged, and it cannot run away from an approaching pointer.
2. **Candidates, in order:** above the box, below it, then to the right and to the left of it (for horizontal bars: right, left, above, below). Along the other axis it is centred on the box and shifted only as far as needed. A candidate is valid when the tooltip lies wholly inside the plot rectangle, inside the viewport and inside every clipping ancestor, and overlaps neither the box nor any control. The first valid candidate is used. For a donut the first candidate is the hole, when the tooltip fits inside it.
3. **A hovered tooltip never takes pointer events.** It is `pointer-events: none`. The plot keeps receiving every move, so picking never stalls at any speed, and a click goes to the plot and selects the datum under the pointer. Moving the pointer onto the tooltip therefore cannot hide it: on line, area and bar the tooltip stays for as long as the pointer's position along the reading axis still picks the same datum, which a straight approach across the reading axis does; on scatter and donut, while the pointer is inside the tooltip's rectangle the datum is held (computed from coordinates in the plot's own move handler, not by letting the tooltip take the event).
3b. **A rest holds the datum along the way to the content (revision 3).** Rule 3 alone lets the content change whenever the straight path to it crosses positions that pick something else, and the final review found such paths for every placement: a tooltip beside a tall bar, a donut's tooltip in the hole, a scatter point's tooltip, a tooltip above a point in a dense line near the plot's edge, and the strip under a small plot. So one rule covers all of them, replacing the per-placement cases of revision 2 (including the unconditional hold inside a scatter or donut tooltip's rectangle, which is withdrawn): once the pointer has rested on a datum for 250 ms (no move larger than 2 CSS px, measured in viewport pixels), that datum is held while the pointer stays inside the corridor between its resting position and the rectangle of the content shown for it (the floating tooltip, or the strip in readout mode), that is, the convex hull of the point and the rectangle, and inside the rectangle itself. Leaving the corridor resumes picking on that same move. A pointer that has not rested is never held, in any placement, so a sweep never stalls.
   - **The hold affects what is shown, never what is activated.** A click or tap always picks afresh from the pointer's position; if that is a different datum from the one held, the click selects and pins the datum under the pointer. A click on empty space (a donut's hole, outside a scatter point's radius) selects nothing.
   - **The hold belongs to one datum, one geometry and one presentation.** It ends when the displayed frame changes that datum's anchor or the content's rectangle, when the presentation switches between floating and strip, on a pin, on Escape, when the pointer leaves the plot and the content, and on any rebuild. After it ends, picking is from the pointer's position at once, without waiting for a move.
4. **Rows are not controls while hovered.** A hovered tooltip is text. Clicking or tapping the plot pins the tooltip for that datum; a pinned tooltip takes pointer events, stays until Escape, a click elsewhere, or its datum leaves the displayed frame, and its rows are buttons of at least 24 × 24 CSS px (WCAG 2.5.8) that select a series. Keyboard focus shows the same tooltip by the same placement; it is never over the focus ring because the box includes the ring.
   - *Revision 3 addendum (two-click range, spec I4):* while the toolbar's Select range toggle is pressed, a click or tap on the plot sets one end of the zoom range instead and neither pins nor selects, and Escape releases the toggle (in rule 7's order after a drag, before a tooltip or a pin).
5. **Readout mode is decided by layout, not by hover.** When the plot, laid out without a strip, would be narrower than 240 CSS px or shorter than 140 CSS px, the figure is in readout mode: a strip of two text lines (two actual line heights of the strip's own font, whatever the page's text size) is reserved under the plot in the layout, and the content that would be in the tooltip is written there as running text ("x: series value; series value; +N more"), wrapping to the two lines and ending in "+N more" when it does not fit; at least the x and one row are always shown. The strip is part of the figure's flow: it covers nothing and nothing covers it. In readout mode there is no floating tooltip. A pinned datum makes the strip's entries buttons of 24 px height. If reserving the strip would leave the plot under the minimum of spec L8 (80 px high), no strip is reserved and pointing shows no readout at all: the datum is still highlighted, and its values are in the keyboard reading and the table. Such a plot is never put into floating mode.
6. **When no candidate is valid outside readout mode** (a tooltip taller than the room around a tall stack, for example), rows are dropped from the end and counted in "+N more" until a candidate is valid. The tooltip is never wider or taller than the visible part of the plot (its content wraps; the visible part is the plot rectangle cut by the viewport and by every clipping ancestor's real clipping edge). If no candidate is valid with one row, the candidate that overlaps the active box least is used, shifted along its free axis as far as needed to avoid every control and every focus ring: controls and focus rings are never covered, in any case. This is the only case in which the active mark may be partly covered, and the table still has every value.
7. Escape dismisses a hovered or pinned tooltip without moving the pointer, until the pointer reaches a different datum. One Escape does one thing: while a tooltip, a pin or a drag is active, the chart consumes the key and nothing else reacts to it (a surrounding dialog stays open, single-series reading stays on); the next Escape goes to whatever is next.
8. **A pin is one datum.** The pin remembers the datum the reader chose. Other data that come to share its position are listed with it while it is displayed; when it leaves the displayed frame or is hidden, the pin ends, whatever else is at that position. A dismissal is remembered for that datum in the same way. With `tooltip: false` nothing can be pinned: a click still selects and takes focus.
9. **Pinned content is real.** A pinned tooltip or strip is exposed to assistive technology with its row buttons named by their text; rows keep their element across redraws while their identity is unchanged, so a press that spans a data update still completes.
10. **Coordinates.** Picking, anchors, clipping and placement use one mapping between the plot's layout pixels and viewport pixels, taken from fractional sizes, so a translated or scaled ancestor (any positive scale, uniform or not) is exact. Rotated, skewed or mirrored ancestors are not supported in 1.0; the limits section of the spec says so.

**Clarifications after the verification** (2026-11-18; the cross-provider check of revision 3, `reviews/2026-11-18/impl/wp/fixes-verify.interaction.review.md`, found these cases unstated; they add no rule, they say what the rules above mean there):

- *An x where no series has a mark* (every value at it is missing): rule 1 has no box to anchor to. The anchor is then the point at that x on the plot's vertical middle (for horizontal bars: at that category on the plot's horizontal middle).
- *The controls of rule 5 and the validity test of rule 2* are the chart's own controls, each taken with its painted focus outline. Controls of the page that happen to overlap the chart are outside what Axylo can know.
- *Several charts on one page and Escape (rule 7):* a chart spends an Escape only when focus is inside its figure, or, when focus is inside no chart, when it is the chart that most recently showed content. One key press is spent by at most one chart.
- *A key that leaves the reader on the same datum* (an arrow at the end of the data, Home on the first point) is not a move: it does not release a pin (rule 4) and does not rewrite the focused text (part 2).
- *A gesture and a pin:* starting a drag or a pinch ends the pin. No state exists in which a pin is held and nothing is shown.
- *A drag while Select range is pressed* zooms as a drag and releases the toggle: the range has been chosen.
- *After Escape from a hold* nothing opens at once: the held datum and the datum under the still pointer are both dismissed. A dismissed datum stays closed until the pointer reaches a datum other than itself (so after moving from one of the two onto the other, that other opens). Escape from a pin or from a plain hover dismisses only the datum on show, not whatever else the pointer is over. The pick itself is always current, so a click activates what is under the pointer.
- *The plot's focus ring* shows when the plot has focus and the last input to it was a key it handles, or when the browser matches `:focus-visible` (which the three engines do after a click on the plot as well). A ring after a click is accepted; what is required is that keyboard use always shows it.
- *Pointer positions are known to one CSS pixel.* Firefox and WebKit report mouse positions in whole pixels (a pointer at 336.96, 82.27 arrives as 336, 82), while the plot's edges and the corridor's edges are fractional. A position up to 1 CSS px outside the plot rectangle is therefore picked as if on its edge, and the corridor of rule 3b is taken with 1 px of slack, so a mark drawn on the plot's edge can be pointed at and a move along the corridor's edge stays inside it in every engine.

Rejected: revision 1; an interactive hovered tooltip with a "safe triangle" (still ambiguous when the reading axis and the approach coincide); always using the readout (loses the association between the values and the mark on plots that have room).

What "can itself be hovered" (spec I1) means under this decision, for the tests: the pointer can be moved straight from the datum onto the tooltip's rectangle, and the tooltip is still shown, for the same datum, when the pointer is inside it. It does not mean the tooltip is the hit-test target.

## 2. The focused point's text changes only for a reason the reader would name

**Problem.** The plot's keyboard proxy is a native range whose value text describes the focused point, ending with its position ("Point 4 of 120"). While data streams in, the count changes on every append, so the text of a focused control changes without the reader acting. Spec A7 forbids unrequested announcements; whether a given screen reader speaks such a change cannot be tested here.

**Rule.** The range's bounds and numeric value are always kept true to the displayed frame, silently. Its value text is rewritten only when:

1. the reader moves (a key, an assistive adjustment, a pointer or touch selection that takes focus),
2. the focused datum's own values change (the same x and series now read differently),
3. the focused datum leaves the frame (the text must then say where focus went), or
4. the plot regains focus.

An append that only changes the count or the ordinal of an unchanged datum does not rewrite the text. The position in the text can therefore be out of date until the next of the four events; it is recomputed then.

To check with a screen reader when one is available (added to decision 0001's list): idle appends with the plot focused are silent; an eviction of the focused point is spoken once; an increment immediately after an append lands on the expected neighbour and reads the current count.

# Phase 1b: Axylo product specification

Revision 3, 2026-11-18. Revised after three independent reviews ([ledger](../reviews/2026-11-18/ledger.md)), then updated with the owner's decisions of the same day: scatter is in 1.0, a compact variant is in 1.0, and the mark renderer is decided by measurement in M1.

Based on the findings in [01-landscape.md](01-landscape.md). Finding IDs (R1–R16 for readers, D1–D10 for developers) refer to that document. Criterion IDs defined here are F, L, I, A (reader), DX (developer) and P (performance).

## 1. What Axylo is

**Axylo is the everyday chart you can ship without checking it.** The smallest correct call produces a chart that represents the data faithfully, stays readable at any width and in any color scheme, and works with a keyboard and a screen reader. When the data is wrong, Axylo says so, to the developer and to the reader, instead of drawing a guess.

It is a framework-neutral TypeScript library under the MIT license. 1.0 ships no framework adapter (owner's decision, 2026-11-18): adapters for React, Vue, Svelte and others come later; in a framework, create the chart when its element exists and call `destroy()` when it goes away.

Speed is a constraint, not the headline: Axylo must stay within the budgets in section 5 with default options. Whether it can do that at a million points with its accessibility layer on is something the first milestone measures, not something this document can promise.

### 1.1 Why someone would choose it

Phase 1 found no library among the ten that holds these together. Each row is the reason to choose Axylo over the library a team would otherwise reach for. The right-hand column is a design target, not a measured result.

| If you would otherwise use | You get today | Axylo aims to add |
|---|---|---|
| Chart.js | Simple API, permissive license, widest reach | Keyboard and screen-reader access without author work; reduced-motion support; a tooltip that appears wherever the pointer is; large data without expert options; a stated time zone on every instant |
| Recharts | The React default | A palette, a title, labels that fit, formatted numbers and dates without code; 100,000 points without seconds of blocking; the same chart outside React |
| Highcharts | The best reader experience of the ten | The same class of accessibility with no module to import and no commercial license; reduced-motion support; errors that name the field and the row |
| ECharts or ApexCharts | Many chart types | Fewer types, each of which fits its labels, reports bad data and is accessible by default |
| uPlot | The speed reference | Automatic sizing, a palette, bars and donuts without path builders, and an accessibility layer, at a speed the budgets in section 5 keep honest |

What Axylo does not try to win: number of chart types, visual customization depth, or exploratory analysis.

### 1.2 Who it is for

A developer adding charts to a product or an internal dashboard: data arrives as rows from an API, the chart is one component among many on the page, and the person writing it is not a visualization specialist and will not test it with a screen reader. Coding agents writing that code are the same audience: they benefit from typed fields, one logical data model and diagnostics that say what to change.

Not the audience for 1.0: analysts exploring data in notebooks, designers building bespoke graphics, and teams that need maps, financial charts or network diagrams.

### 1.3 Principles

| Principle | In practice |
|---|---|
| Correct before configurable | A default that can mislead (truncated bars, interpolated gaps, a silently dropped label) is a bug, even if an option fixes it. |
| Say it, do not guess | Anything Axylo cannot draw faithfully becomes a diagnostic with a code, a location and a fix. If values were left out, the reader is told too. |
| The data is the authority | Exact values, the table, keyboard navigation and descriptions come from the normalized data. The drawing is derived from it and may be simplified; nothing else may be. |
| Everything a reader needs is on; nothing else is | Title, units, legend, tooltip, keyboard, description and table are on. Entry animation, a marker on every point of a dense line, and decorative toolbars are not. |
| One way to do each thing | One logical data model, one method per kind of change, one place for colors (CSS). |
| The page is the theme | Font, text color and color scheme come from the page. |

## 2. Scope of the first release

### 2.1 Chart types

| Type | Variants | Typical question | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Line | Multi-series, gaps; time, date, numeric or category x | How did it change? | 1.0 |
| Bar | Vertical, horizontal, grouped, stacked | How do categories compare? | 1.0 |
| Area | Single, stacked | How did the total and its parts change? | 1.0 |
| Donut | Up to eight slices | What share does each part have? | 1.0 |
| Scatter | Optional series | How are two measures related? | 1.0 (owner's decision) |
| Compact variant | Of line, area and bar: marks only, for KPI tiles and sparklines | Which way is it going? | 1.0 (owner's decision) |

Plus, on every cartesian chart: reference lines and bands (a target, an incident window).

The Phase 1 harness exercised line, bar and donut in all ten libraries (donut in nine; uPlot has none). Area and scatter are added on judgment; Phase 1 found no usage data by chart type. Two reviewers argued for fewer types and one for a compact variant; the owner decided on all five types plus the compact variant. Scatter alone needs two-dimensional hit testing and its own navigation model, so it is built last and carries the most schedule risk.

Each type has its own rules for picking, navigation and limits. They are in the type matrix in section 3.6, and a type does not ship until its row is fully tested.

### 2.2 Workflows

| # | Workflow | What it requires of Axylo |
|---|---|---|
| W1 | Show a query result | Rows in, chart out; field types inferred where that is safe; bad rows reported. |
| W2 | Fill a dashboard | Dozens of charts per page; container-sized; themed by the page; loading, empty and error states; a chart can take its name from the card's own heading. |
| W3 | Compare categories | Long labels; horizontal bars; grouped and stacked. |
| W4 | Watch a live metric | Append without redraw cost growing; a pause control; no announcement flood. |
| W5 | Explore a range | Tooltip anywhere, legend toggle, zoom and pan by single click, drag, touch and keyboard. |
| W6 | Read it another way | Keyboard, screen reader, table view, high contrast, reduced motion, 400% zoom, color-vision deficiency. |

### 2.3 Supported environments

| Dimension | 1.0 |
|---|---|
| Browsers | The current and previous major versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari (macOS and iOS). |
| TypeScript | 5.4 and later. Plain JavaScript is fully supported; types are an aid, not a requirement. |
| Frameworks | None needed. No adapter ships in 1.0; the library is called from any framework's mount and unmount hooks. |
| Text direction | Left-to-right pages. Right-to-left text renders, but the layout is not mirrored; this is stated in the conformance table. |
| Transformed ancestors | A chart inside a translated or scaled ancestor (any positive scale, uniform or not) is exact. Inside a rotated, skewed or mirrored ancestor it draws, but pointer picking and tooltip placement are wrong; this is not supported in 1.0 and the documentation says so (decision 0004, rule 10). |
| Built-in text | English, overridable (A10). |
